title: Cauchy's Theorem: a Prime Divisor of |G| is Realized as an Element Order
description: Lagrange's theorem says every subgroup order divides |G|; its naive converse is false (A₄ has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6). Cauchy's theorem provides the converse for prime divisors: if a prime p divides |G|, then G has an element of order exactly p, hence a cyclic subgroup of order p. This entry restates Mathlib's Cauchy theorem and assembles the standard converse-to-Lagrange package: the subgroup form, the equivalence 'p | |G| ⟺ p | exp(G)', the resulting equality of prime factors of |G| and exp(G), and the p = 2 special case (even order ⟺ contains an involution), witnessed concretely in S₃.

overview.historicalContext: Cauchy proved in 1845 that a finite group whose order is divisible by a prime p contains an element of order p — the first genuine converse to Lagrange's 1770s divisibility theorem, and the historical seed of the Sylow theorems (1872), which extend it from p to every prime power p^k dividing |G|. In a modern algebra course Cauchy's theorem is the pivot between 'orders of subgroups divide |G|' (Lagrange, easy) and 'which divisors are actually attained' (hard, and false in general): the alternating group A₄ is the standard counterexample, having order 12 yet no subgroup of order 6. Cauchy isolates exactly the part of the converse that always holds — the prime divisors.
overview.problemStatement: Lagrange's theorem constrains subgroup orders to divide |G|. To what extent does the divisibility admit a converse — for which divisors d of |G| is there guaranteed to be a subgroup (or element) of order d? Determine the sharp prime-divisor answer and its equivalent formulations in terms of element orders, cyclic subgroups, and the group exponent.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Cauchy as the engine.** Mathlib supplies exists_prime_orderOf_dvd_card': for a finite group, a prime p dividing Nat.card G yields x with orderOf x = p. We wrap it to take primality as an ordinary hypothesis.

**Subgroup form.** The cyclic subgroup zpowers x generated by such an x has Nat.card (zpowers x) = orderOf x = p (Nat.card_zpowers), and a group of prime order is cyclic (isCyclic_of_prime_card). So every prime divisor is realized by a cyclic subgroup of that order.

**Exponent equivalence.** p | |G| ⟹ p | exp(G) because the order-p element's order divides the exponent (order_dvd_exponent). Conversely p | exp(G) ⟹ p | |G| because exp(G) | |G| (Group.exponent_dvd_nat_card). This iff upgrades to primeFactors (|G|) = primeFactors (exp(G)) via Nat.mem_primeFactors, using that both numbers are nonzero for a finite group.

**The p = 2 case.** Specializing to p = 2 gives: even order ⟺ an involution exists. Forward is Cauchy at 2; reverse is Lagrange (orderOf x = 2 divides |G|). Concretely S₃ = Perm (Fin 3) has order 3! = 6, exhibiting both a transposition (order 2) and a 3-cycle (order 3).
keyInsights: Cauchy is exactly the prime-divisor slice of the (otherwise false) converse to Lagrange. The A₄ counterexample shows the composite case genuinely fails, so 'prime' is not a convenience hypothesis but the sharp boundary.

The exponent equivalence 'p | |G| ⟺ p | exp(G)' packages Cauchy and its easy converse into a single statement, and yields the striking fact that |G| and exp(G) — which can differ wildly in size — never differ in their prime factors.
Every prime divisor is witnessed not just by an element but by a cyclic subgroup of that prime order, because an order-p element generates a group of prime order and prime-order groups are cyclic.

The classical 'even order groups have involutions' result is not a separate theorem but the p = 2 instance of Cauchy, and the reverse implication is pure Lagrange — making the iff a clean microcosm of the whole converse story.

conclusion.summary: Restated Cauchy's theorem and assembled the sharp prime-divisor converse to Lagrange: a prime p divides |G| iff G has an element of order p iff G has a cyclic subgroup of order p iff p divides exp(G). This yields the equality of prime-factor sets primeFactors(|G|) = primeFactors(exp(G)), and specializes at p = 2 to 'even order ⟺ contains an involution', witnessed concretely in S₃. 179 lines, 9 theorems, 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: Cauchy is the exact boundary of the converse to Lagrange: for prime divisors it holds unconditionally, while the A₄ counterexample shows the composite case fails. The exponent formulation records that |G| and exp(G) share prime factors, and the involution corollary is the algebraic backbone of results like 'a group of even order has a non-identity element equal to its own inverse'. The prime-order cyclic subgroup produced here is also the first step toward Sylow theory, which extends Cauchy from primes to prime powers.
openQuestions: Formalize the sharpness witness explicitly: prove that A₄ (or Alternating (Fin 4)) has order 12 but no subgroup of order 6, certifying that the converse to Lagrange genuinely fails for composite divisors.
State and prove the Sylow strengthening in the same Nat.card idiom: for every prime power p^k dividing |G| there is a subgroup of order p^k, recovering Cauchy as the k = 1 case.
